new_task_1.title: Preserve outer variable visibility in `for`-`else` blocks
new_task_1.description: The compiler no longer injects synthetic generator scaffolding into ordinary unbuffered blocks, which fixes a scoping bug where a `for` loop's target name could incorrectly shadow an outer variable inside the loop's `else` branch when the loop did not iterate.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that a `for` loop with an `else` branch does not hide an outer variable that uses the same name as the loop target when the loop body never runs.

expectation.grounded: When compiling an unbuffered `for` block and its `else` branch, Jinja must not emit dummy `yield` code solely to force generator shape. If a template renders `{% for item in [] %}{% else %}{{ item }}{% endfor %}` with an outer `item` value in context, the `else` branch should resolve that outer `item` value instead of treating the loop target as a locally shadowing name with no bound value.
expectation.conceptual: If a loop never assigns its target because it never iterates, the `else` branch should still be able to see an outer variable with that same name.

constraints.grounded: The change must preserve normal `for`-loop rendering, loop-variable binding during actual iteration, and existing behavior for empty blocks that still need valid generated Python code. It should only remove the synthetic generator side effect that altered scope behavior in non-iterating cases.
constraints.conceptual: Keep normal loop execution intact while fixing the accidental name-shadowing edge case in the `else` path.

behavior: A `for` loop that does not iterate no longer causes its target name to shadow an outer variable of the same name inside the `else` branch.
The `else` branch resolves names using the surrounding template scope when the loop body never binds the loop target.
Normal loop-target binding during real iterations remains unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: When a template renders `{% for item in [] %}{% else %}{{ item }}{% endfor %}` with `item=42` in the surrounding context, it should render `42`.
When a `for` loop does iterate, references to the loop target inside the loop body should continue to use the iterated value.
When a block is otherwise empty, generated template code should remain syntactically valid without reintroducing the scoping regression.

new_task_2.title: Expand `title` filter word boundaries around punctuation
new_task_2.description: The `title` filter now recognizes additional punctuation-delimited word starts, so words inside constructs like parentheses, braces, brackets, and angle brackets are title-cased instead of remaining lowercase after the opening delimiter.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that the `title` filter capitalizes words that begin immediately after common opening punctuation, not only words separated by whitespace or hyphens.

expectation.grounded: The implementation of `do_title` must split input using the broader word-beginning regex used by Jinja's filters rather than only splitting on hyphens and whitespace. As a result, inputs such as `foo (bar)`, `foo {bar}`, `foo [bar]`, and `foo <bar>` must render as `Foo (Bar)`, `Foo {Bar}`, `Foo [Bar]`, and `Foo <Bar>` respectively.
expectation.conceptual: Title-casing should treat words after common opening punctuation as new words.

constraints.grounded: Existing title-casing behavior for whitespace-separated, tab-separated, and hyphen-separated words must continue to work. The filter should still lowercase the remainder of each word segment after uppercasing the initial character.
constraints.conceptual: This should extend the filter's notion of word boundaries without regressing its existing formatting rules.

behavior: Words immediately following `(`, `{`, `[`, or `<` are title-cased by the `title` filter.
Existing title-casing for words separated by spaces, tabs, or hyphens remains intact.
The filter continues to uppercase the first character of each detected word segment and lowercase the remaining characters in that segment.

new_task_3.title: Add `greaterthan` and `lessthan` built-in tests
new_task_3.description: Jinja 2.9 adds two new built-in test names, `greaterthan` and `lessthan`, which expose direct comparison checks through the template `is` test mechanism.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates can express greater-than and less-than comparisons through named built-in tests in addition to the existing comparison operators.

expectation.grounded: The built-in `TESTS` registry must include `greaterthan` and `lessthan` entries that evaluate `value > other` and `value < other` respectively. Templates using `is greaterthan(...)` or `is lessthan(...)` should resolve these names without requiring custom test registration.
expectation.conceptual: Template authors should be able to write readable named comparison tests for greater-than and less-than checks.

constraints.grounded: Existing built-in tests and comparison-operator behavior must remain unchanged. The new tests should follow the same argument-passing rules as other built-in tests and should not require new syntax beyond normal `is` test usage.
constraints.conceptual: This should extend the standard test vocabulary without altering how existing tests or operators behave.

behavior: Templates can use `is greaterthan(value)` as a built-in test.
Templates can use `is lessthan(value)` as a built-in test.
The new tests evaluate using the normal Python comparison semantics for `>` and `<`.
acceptance_criteria: A template condition like `{% if n is greaterthan(3) %}` should evaluate true when `n` is greater than `3`.
A template condition like `{% if n is lessthan(3) %}` should evaluate true when `n` is less than `3`.
Templates that do not use the new test names should continue to behave as before.

new_task_4.title: Add `Node.dump()` for AST inspection
new_task_4.description: The low-level AST node API now exposes `Node.dump()`, which returns a recursive string representation of a parsed node tree for debugging and inspection.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that callers working with Jinja's parsed AST can obtain a readable serialized representation of node trees without building their own traversal logic.

expectation.grounded: Instances of `jinja2.nodes.Node` must expose a `dump()` method that recursively formats the node tree as a string using `nodes.<ClassName>(...)` notation, descending into child nodes and lists of child nodes and using `repr(...)` for non-node literal values.
expectation.conceptual: The parsed AST should have a built-in debug view that is easy to print and inspect.

constraints.grounded: The output should recurse through the node's declared fields in order, include nested lists inline, and work for nodes with no fields by returning a closed `nodes.<ClassName>()` form. The method should not require external serializer helpers.
constraints.conceptual: This should be a simple, direct inspection API for low-level consumers rather than a behavior change to template rendering.

behavior: Parsed AST nodes expose a `dump()` method.
Calling `dump()` returns a recursive textual representation of the node and its children.
Literal values inside the tree are represented with their Python `repr` output.
acceptance_criteria: When application code parses a template and calls `dump()` on the resulting AST node, it should receive a string rather than needing a separate visitor.
When a node contains nested child nodes or lists of child nodes, the returned string should include those descendants recursively.
When a node has no declared fields, `dump()` should still return a valid `nodes.<ClassName>()` representation.
